Australia trimmed mean CPI jumps to 3.8% in October, keeping further RBA hike risk alive
body: The core beat should support the Australian dollar and push front-end yields higher as traders trim bets on 2027 rate cuts and price in some risk of another hike. December pricing is unlikely to change much, given the weak labour market and the RBA's view that policy is already restrictive. The bigger shift is for the February meeting, which now looks more open. A firmer AUD would ease some imported inflation pressure, while rate-sensitive sectors on the ASX, including property and consumer discretionary, may come under pressure if markets price a longer period of high rates.

Australian core inflation rose further from target in October, leaving a December hold the likeliest outcome but putting further RBA hikes back in play for 2027 and pushing rate-cut hopes further out.

Australia's underlying inflation accelerated more than expected in October, with the Reserve Bank of Australia's preferred trimmed mean measure rising to 3.8% from a year earlier, up from 3.6% in September and above the 3.6% forecast, according to figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics. The trimmed mean climbed 0.5% over the month, outpacing expectations of 0.3% and the 0.3% gain the previous month.

Headline inflation also topped forecasts, rising 0.5% in the month to take the annual rate to 4.9%, up from 4.3% and above the 4.7% expected. Higher fuel prices and the unwinding of electricity subsidies had been flagged as the main drivers of the headline increase, but the strength of the core measures points to broader price pressure. The weighted median, another underlying gauge, held at 3.4% year on year, with a 0.3% monthly rise.

The figures challenge the view, widely held ahead of the release, that October would mark the peak in inflation. The RBA's own November forecasts had headline inflation topping out at 4.5%, and the trimmed mean is now further above the bank's 2% to 3% target range than it was a month ago.

The RBA has raised its cash rate by 125 basis points this year, to 4.85%, as inflation stayed well above target. Its November decision was split, with three of nine board members preferring to hold, and the statement dropped its warning that further increases might be needed. A sharp rise in unemployment to 4.9% in October had since reinforced expectations that the tightening cycle was over.

A hold at the 7 to 8 December meeting still looks the most likely outcome, given the weakening labour market and the RBA's assessment that policy is now clearly restrictive. However, with core inflation moving further from target, further rate increases cannot be ruled out. The board's first decision of 2027 is due on 9 February, with two more monthly inflation reports due before then, and those figures are likely to determine whether the October jump proves a one-off or the start of a more persistent trend. Markets that had priced a first rate cut in the second half of 2027 may need to push that timing back.
Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Bullock facing stagflationary pressures.

news.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6559 – Reuters estimate
body: The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets.

China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours.

Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations.

Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks.

As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.

In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

news.title: US PCE preview: inflation seen near 3.8% in the Fed's last read before a December hike
body: With a December hike largely priced, the reaction is more likely to come through expectations for early 2027. A core print of 0.4% or more would probably lift front-end Treasury yields and the dollar as traders add to bets on follow-up hikes in January or March. A 0.2% reading would ease that pressure without removing the December move. Gold is exposed to a hot print, since higher rate expectations have weighed on it throughout this tightening cycle. Thin Thanksgiving liquidity adds to the risk of outsized moves across FX, bonds and equity futures.

A December Fed hike looks all but settled, so Wednesday's October PCE report is really about what comes next, with a firm core reading likely to strengthen the case for further tightening early in 2027.

The US October personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, due at 13:30 GMT (8:30am US Eastern) on Wednesday, is the last major inflation reading the Federal Reserve will see before its 9 December decision, and it arrives with a rate hike already largely priced. The question for markets is less whether the Fed tightens in December than how far it goes after that. Headline PCE inflation is expected to rise to around 3.8% year on year from 3.6% in September, in line with the Cleveland Fed's inflation nowcast, while core PCE, which strips out food and energy and is the Fed's preferred gauge, is seen edging up to around 3.2% from 3.1%.

The monthly core number is likely to drive the reaction. Most forecasts sit near 0.3%, with Goldman Sachs at 0.3% after trimming its estimate, and some research houses as high as 0.4%. Fed Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman said earlier this month that progress on inflation appeared to have stalled and that she expected annual core PCE of around 3.3% for October.

This report carries extra weight because October's consumer price index was published without an annual rate. Price collection was disrupted during the 2025 government shutdown, leaving no year-ago base, so PCE provides the only year-on-year inflation measure for October. That CPI report showed monthly gains of 0.4% for the headline and 0.3% for core, both a tenth above forecasts, while producer prices have been running at their fastest annual pace since late 2022.

The Fed raised rates in September to a 3.75% to 4.00% target range and held in October in a 10 to 2 vote, with two dissenters preferring a hike. Futures put the odds of a quarter-point increase in December at around 90%. Goldman Sachs expects hikes in December and March, while Bank of America sees three quarter-point increases in December, January and March, so a firm core reading would mainly feed into expectations for the early months of 2027.

Several other releases land at the same time, including the second estimate of third-quarter GDP, weekly jobless claims brought forward because of Thanksgiving, and personal income and spending. The Fed's Beige Book follows at 19:00 GMT. With US equity markets closed on Thursday and closing early on Friday, thin holiday liquidity could amplify any surprise.

news.title: JPMorgan's 8,200 S&P 500 target for 2027 sits below peers as Fed risk tempers AI upside
body: A major bank calling the recent tech sell-off a better entry point could support dip buying in AI-linked megacaps, though the below-consensus target also argues for keeping expectations in check. Rate-sensitive sectors look most exposed to the risk JPMorgan names, and so do richly valued growth names, if Fed tightening pushes financial conditions tighter still. For futures traders, the note adds to a two-sided view: positioning has reset, but sentiment is fragile and liquidity thinner, which could keep volatility high through year-end.
JPMorgan still sees AI earnings lifting US stocks through 2027, but its 8,200 target leaves less room than rival banks' targets do for a Fed that stays tight.

JPMorgan expects the S&P 500 to end 2027 at 8,200, a gain of about 14% from current levels, but its target sits at the cautious end of Wall Street forecasts as rising US interest rates cloud the outlook. The call, from the bank's global markets strategy team led by Dubravko Lakos-Bujas, is below a consensus of around 8,470 compiled by Bloomberg, and well short of the 8,700 year-end targets set by strategists at Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley. It is in line with forecasts from UBS Global Wealth Management, Wells Fargo and Bank of America.

The strategists remain constructive on the earnings picture. They expect above-trend profit growth tied to what they describe as an AI supercycle, arguing that demand for computing power and the rapid pace of technical progress should support another year of heavy AI investment. In their view, the AI cycle is broadly intact despite recent doubts over the pace and financing of that spending.

They also see an opportunity in the recent sell-off. A momentum unwind and a broader reset in positioning have, the team argues, improved the near-term risk-reward for equities. The S&P 500 is up nearly 5% this year but roughly 8% below its October record near 7,840, with AI-linked stocks leading the decline.

The restraint in the target comes from the policy backdrop. Higher interest rates and uncertainty around AI following the US midterm elections have weighed on sentiment, and the strategists see a gradual recovery only if the Federal Reserve gives more weight to its growth mandate alongside price stability. The main risk they identify is collateral damage from monetary tightening, at a time when financial conditions and liquidity have already worsened and investor sentiment remains fragile.

That framing puts the Fed at the centre of the 2027 equity story. With the central bank on a hiking path, one reading of JPMorgan's call is that earnings can still carry US stocks higher, but with less help from rising valuations than its more bullish peers may be counting on. The gap between the 8,200 and 8,700 camps is likely to narrow or widen depending on how quickly inflation eases and whether the Fed signals that its tightening is close to an end.

news.title: investingLive Americas FX news wrap 24 Nov: It’s a Wrap. Chip stocks slide. Anthropic breaks IPO price. USD lower.
body: Monday’s Nvidia-led rally lost momentum Tuesday. Chip and AI infrastructure shares took the brunt of the selling, and Anthropic finished below its $83 IPO price after briefly trading back above it. The Dow and Russell 2000 held up as the Nasdaq slid.

A report that the Trump administration is preparing fresh tariffs on China, the EU and 14 other economies put import costs and inflation back in focus. Here we go again. I smell Steven Miller - new Chief of Staff - exerting his pressure on Trump images.investinglive.com
Treasury yields edged higher, led by the 2-year, while the dollar fell against most of the majors. Oil rebounded as gold, silver and Bitcoin moved lower.

The USD was weakest against the Swiss franc and strongest against the Japanese yen. USDCHF fell 0.72% to 0.8354, while USDJPY rose 0.14% to 159.23. USDCAD fell 0.63% to 1.4268. Higher oil helped support the loonie, and Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem said the Bank may need to respond sooner or more forcefully to large or persistent supply shocks. The renewed policy framework keeps the 2% inflation target. images.investinglive.com
EURUSD rose 0.58% to 1.0964, GBPUSD gained 0.61% to 1.3110, AUDUSD rose 0.21% to 0.6640 and NZDUSD gained 0.61% to 0.5482.

The 2s10s curve flattened modestly. Firmer confidence and higher oil were consistent with the front end leading the move. The $70 billion 5-year auction stopped at 4.719% with a small tail and a 2.37x bid-to-cover ratio. Direct bidders took 36.7%, helping offset softer indirect demand. investinglive.com

Nvidia fell 5.86% to $155.38 after surging 31.48% on Monday following Jensen Huang’s return as CEO. The selling was heavier across parts of the AI trade. Astera Labs fell 13.88%, Credo lost 13.07%, Micron fell 10.97% and AI cloud provider CoreWeave dropped 11.85%. Apple gained 1.43% and Microsoft added 0.74%. The S&P 500’s 0.49% decline masked how hard the chip and AI infrastructure names were hit. investinglive.com

Anthropic finished at $81.91, down 6.54%. It traded as low as $75.61 and as high as $83.49. That makes the $83 IPO price the first barometer for the next session. Buyers got above it briefly today, then gave it back.

November consumer confidence jumped to 103.3 from a revised 91.9, with both current conditions and expectations improving. The Richmond Fed manufacturing index rose to +3 from −2 as new orders rebounded. Firms reported faster input-cost growth, while selling-price growth held steady. investinglive.com

September FHFA house prices were flat month over month versus +0.2% expected. The Case-Shiller 20-city index rose 2.6% year over year versus 2.7% expected. National Bank of Canada economist Jocelyn Paquet highlighted the squeeze on builders. High mortgage rates are holding back demand, residential construction input prices are up nearly 60% since the pandemic began, and builder sentiment is at its lowest since 2012. The AI investment boom has helped mask how much higher rates are weighing on housing. investinglive.com InvestingLive’s housing analysis

WTI settled at $82.05, up $1.88 or 2.35%, then eased to $81.40, up 1.53%, in the later snapshot. The settlement was two cents above the falling 100-hour moving average at $82.03. The pullback put WTI back below it, leaving $82.03 as the barometer for whether buyers can build on the rebound. Iranian state media reported that the army commander called for tighter control of the Strait of Hormuz until Tehran’s conditions are met, keeping supply risks in focus. investinglive.com WTI settlement and technicals

Spot gold fell 2.30% to $3,551.02, while silver slid 5.59% to $40.729. Gold got little help from the softer dollar as Treasury yields edged higher. Silver and copper both fell more than 4%, consistent with broader selling across metals. For gold buyers, the 100-hour moving average remains the first hurdle after another rejection. images.investinglive.com Gold technical analysis
Bitcoin was down 2.57% at $59,638 late in the session. It traded with the Nasdaq and other risk-sensitive assets as the bounce that followed Monday’s Nvidia news faded. images.investinglive.com

The first question is whether buyers return to the chip stocks and whether Anthropic can get back above $83 and stay there. Watch $82.03 in WTI alongside the pending tariff details. A move back above $60,000 in Bitcoin would be another sign that buyers are returning to risk-sensitive assets.

news.title: Australia CPI preview: 4.8% looks like the peak, but the core print will move the RBA
body: The headline rise is largely priced in, so the Australian dollar and short-dated Australian government bond yields are more exposed to the core reading. The Aussie is trading around 66.4 US cents. A trimmed mean of 0.4% or firmer would likely lift front-end yields and support the currency by pushing back expectations for the first rate cut. A 0.3% print would leave in place the banks' expected easing timeline for mid-to-late 2027. US markets are heading into a Thanksgiving-shortened week, so any AUD move may meet thinner liquidity than usual. For energy watchers, the fuel-led headline is another sign of crude prices feeding into inflation and central bank decisions well beyond the US.

Australia's October consumer price index, due at 00:30 GMT on Wednesday (7:30pm US Eastern on Tuesday), is expected to show headline inflation at what forecasters see as the top of the current cycle. The core reading will shape expectations for when the Reserve Bank of Australia can begin cutting rates. Consensus has headline CPI rising 0.4% over the month, taking the annual rate to 4.8% from 4.3% in September. Forecasts for the trimmed mean, the RBA's preferred core gauge, are less settled. Most calls are at 0.3% m/m with the annual rate holding at 3.6%, while several forecasters see 0.4% and a lift to 3.7%.

The big four banks are split down the middle. Commonwealth Bank and NAB both see headline at 4.7% and the trimmed mean steady at 3.6%. Westpac and ANZ are at 4.8% and 3.7%. In its preview, Westpac forecast monthly gains of around 0.4% for both headline and core and described October as the likely peak in Australian inflation, with the trimmed mean expected to slip below 3% by the third quarter of 2027.

Fuel does most of the work on the headline. NAB estimates higher automotive fuel prices will add around 1.2 points to year-end inflation, and the unwinding of government electricity subsidies adds to the rise. Neither is the kind of domestic demand pressure that monetary policy is designed to lean against. A wildcard sits in the core: card payment surcharges were banned from 1 October, and it is unclear how many businesses folded that cost into their prices. ANZ estimates the change could add about 0.1 point to headline CPI.

The labour market has turned sharply. Unemployment rose to 4.9% in October, its highest since 2021, after a similar upside surprise in September, and the economy shed jobs in both months. At its November meeting the RBA lifted the cash rate to 4.85%, but three of the nine board members preferred to hold, and the statement afterwards no longer flagged further increases.

Markets price a hold at the 7 to 8 December meeting as near certain, and all four major banks expect one. That makes today's numbers a guide to the timing of the first cut, which the banks currently place between June and August 2027. A 0.3% core print would support the view that inflation has peaked and keep mid-2027 easing in sight. A 0.4% or firmer reading would suggest underlying price pressure is fading too slowly for the board to ease soon, even as job losses mount.
